question: NPC: A question with a yes-or-no answer
intro: Nia stands at a tavern door with a slate in her hand. “A program that treats everyone the same is a vending machine. To do better it has to ask a question — and the question has to have a yes-or-no answer.”

steps.say: This is an if statement. The part in round brackets is the condition. When it is true, the code inside the braces runs; when it is false, that code is skipped.

beats.say: This is an if statement. The part in round brackets is the condition.
When the condition is true, the code inside the braces runs. When it is false, that code is skipped and the program carries on below the closing brace.

check.prompt: isRegular is changed to false. What does this code print now?
check.why: A false condition means the braces are skipped entirely. An if on its own does nothing in that case.

steps.say: The condition has to be something that is true or false: a boolean variable, or a comparison such as age >= 21. A number or a piece of text on its own will not do.

beats.say: The condition has to be something that is true or false: a boolean variable, or a comparison.

beats.code:
if (age >= 21) { ... }     // fine: a comparison
if (isRegular) { ... }     // fine: a boolean variable
if (25) { ... }            // refused: 25 is not true or false

check.prompt: coins is an int. Which of these can be the condition of an if?
check.why: coins > 10 is a comparison, so its answer is true or false. coins + 10 and coins are just numbers, and Java will not treat a number as yes or no.

steps.say: Two pieces of punctuation are not optional here: the round brackets around the condition, and the braces around the code it controls.

beats.say: Two pieces of punctuation are not optional here: the round brackets around the condition, and the braces around the code it controls.

outro: “Condition in brackets, code in braces. The next monsters want to know when the braces are entered and when they are skipped.”

question: The condition of this if is a boolean variable. What does the program print?
feedback: isRegular is false, so the code inside the braces is skipped. The last line is outside the braces, so it runs whatever the condition was. An if never stops the program; it only decides whether its own block runs.

question: age is an int, hasID is a boolean and name is a String. Which of these can be used as the condition of an if?
incorrect: age + 21
name
feedback: A condition has to be true or false. A comparison such as age >= 21 gives a boolean, and hasID already is one. age + 21 and 21 are numbers, and name is text: Java will not treat any of those as a yes or a no, and the compiler rejects them.

question:
The compiler rejects this line. What is wrong with it?
if hasID {
correct: The condition is not inside round brackets
incorrect: The condition is not a comparison with ==
The line does not end with a semicolon
The brace should come on the line below
feedback: In Java the condition of an if always goes in round brackets: if (hasID) { . A boolean variable is a perfectly good condition without any ==. A line that opens a block with { takes no semicolon, and the brace may sit on the same line.

incorrect: "true"
feedback: A comparison such as age >= 18 is an expression in its own right, and its value is a boolean: true or false. It can be stored, printed or combined like any other value, not just placed inside an if. adult does not hold the age that was tested, only the verdict. Java does not use 1 and 0 for true and false, and "true" in quotes would be a String, which is a different type.

question: Work out the condition first, then choose the block. What does this program print?
feedback: 19 >= 21 is false, so the first block is skipped and the else block runs. With an if-else exactly one of the two blocks runs: the first when the condition is true, the else when it is false.

question: A chain of conditions is checked from the top. What does this program print?
feedback: 18 < 17 is false, so Java moves on to the next condition. 18 < 19 is true, so that block runs and the rest of the chain is skipped. The second test did not need to say “17 or later”: it is only ever reached when the first test has already failed.

question: A score of 85 is supposed to earn "good". What does this chain actually print?
feedback: An if / else if chain is checked from the top, and the first true condition wins: its branch runs and the rest of the chain is skipped without being tested. 85 >= 60 is true, so pass is printed and "good" is never reached. The fix is to test the most demanding condition first: >= 90, then >= 80, then >= 60.

question: An if / else if / else if chain ends with a final else, so it has four blocks. How many of them run each time the chain is reached?
incorrect: At least one of the four
Every one whose test is true
None, one or several of them
feedback: Java checks the conditions from the top and runs the block of the FIRST one that is true; the rest of the chain is skipped without being tested. If none is true, the final else runs. Either way exactly one block runs. (Without the final else, it could be none.)

prompt: Fill in the keywords that join this chain together.
feedback: else if adds another condition to the chain, tested only when everything above it was false. A plain else has no condition at all: it catches whatever is left. That is why the last block needs no test for “21 or over”.

feedback_template: There is no else here, so these are four separate if statements, and every one of them is tested. Each condition that {{s}} satisfies adds a star, giving {{expected}}. In an else-if chain only the first true branch would run, and stars could never pass 1.

question: age is an int. Match each condition to what it asks.
feedback: == asks “equal to” and != asks “not equal to”. > and < leave the number itself out, so age > 21 starts at 22. >= and <= include it. Whether the boundary value counts is the most common mistake in a condition, so check it every time.

question:
What happens when this line is compiled?
if (age = 21) {
correct: It is refused: = stores a value and does not compare
incorrect: It compiles, and is true whenever age equals 21
It compiles, and is true for any value of age
It is refused: 21 has to be written in quotes
feedback: A single = is assignment: it would put 21 into age, and the result is a number, not true or false — so the compiler rejects it as a condition. To compare, use two: if (age == 21). Remember it as “= stores, == asks”.

question: age is an int. Write the condition (just the condition: no if, no brackets, no semicolon) that is true when age is 21 or more.
feedback: age >= 21 — “greater than or equal to”, so 21 itself counts. age > 21 would turn away someone who is exactly 21. (age > 20 says the same thing for whole numbers, but >= 21 says what you mean.)

question: NPC: Both, or either
intro: Nia chalks two words on the door: AND, OR. “One test is often not enough. The door wants an ID and the right age. The late hours want a weekend or a holiday. Java has one operator for each of those words.”

steps.say: && means AND: the whole condition is true only when BOTH sides are true. One false side is enough to make it false.

beats.say: && means AND. The whole condition is true only when BOTH sides are true. One false side is enough to make it false.

check.prompt: hasID is true and age is 19. What is  hasID && age >= 21 ?
check.why: The left side is true, but 19 >= 21 is false, and && needs both. So the whole condition is false.

steps.say: || means OR: true when AT LEAST ONE side is true, including when both are. It is false only when both sides are false.

beats.say: || means OR. The condition is true when AT LEAST ONE side is true — including when both are. It is false only when both sides are false.

check.prompt: isWeekend is false and isHoliday is true. What is  isWeekend || isHoliday ?
check.why: One true side is all || needs. It does not matter which side it is.

steps.say: When you mix the two, use parentheses to say which tests belong together.

beats.say: When you mix the two, use parentheses to say which tests belong together.
Read the parentheses first: a regular who has spent 10 — or anyone at all who has spent 25.

outro: “Both for &&, either for ||. The next monsters give you the values; you give the verdict.”

question: x is an int. Match each rule, written in English, to the Java condition that implements it.

pairs.term: x is between 1 and 10, including both ends
x is outside the range 1 to 10

feedback: "Between" needs both tests to hold, so it is && (AND). "Outside" is satisfied by either side, so it is || (OR). "Neither 1 nor 10" means not 1 AND not 10: writing x != 1 || x != 10 would be true for every number, because no number equals both. Including the ends means >= and <=; strictly between means > and <.

question: && needs both of its sides to be true. What does this program print?
feedback: hasID is true, but 19 >= 21 is false. && is true only when BOTH sides are, so the whole condition is false and the else block runs. Having an ID is not enough by itself.

Work out each side, then join them. && needs both sides true: 5 < 10 and 10 > 7 are both true, but a > b is false, which sinks a > b && b == 10. || needs only one side true: b == 10 rescues the second, a < b rescues the third, and a == b || b < 7 has nothing true on either side.

prompt: Fill in the operator each rule needs.
question:
if (hasID {{1}} age >= 21) {          // needs an ID and the right age

if (isWeekend {{2}} isHoliday) {      // either one is enough
feedback: “And” in the rule means &&: both conditions have to hold. “Either” means ||: one is enough. Both operators are written with the symbol doubled.

question: hour is an int. Happy hour runs from 17 up to, but not including, 19. Write the condition (no if, no semicolon) that is true during happy hour.
feedback: hour >= 17 && hour < 19. A range needs two comparisons, one for each end, joined with && because both have to hold. Each comparison names hour again: Java has no way to write 17 <= hour < 19 in one piece.

correct: It does not compile: 0 < x is a boolean, and a boolean cannot be compared with 10
incorrect: It prints in range, because Java reads this as 0 < x and x < 10
It prints in range for any x, because 0 < x becomes 0 or 1, and both are below 10
It compiles, but throws an exception when the comparison is evaluated
feedback: Java evaluates 0 < x first and gets a boolean. The next step would be true < 10, and < does not accept a boolean, so the compiler rejects the line ("bad operand types"). The maths notation has to be written as two tests joined with AND: 0 < x && x < 10. (In C the chained form compiles and is quietly wrong; Java refuses it.)

question: Read the parentheses first. What does this program print?
feedback: Inside the parentheses: isRegular is true and 15.0 >= 10 is true, so that part is true. || needs only one true side, so the whole condition is true without spent >= 25 mattering at all.

question: NPC: One name, many boxes
intro: Zoya slides a long rack of numbered pigeonholes onto the bench. “Five drinks, five variables. Then the landlord adds twenty more. An array is one name for a whole row of boxes.”

steps.say: The square brackets after the type say: this is an array of Strings. The braces list what goes in the boxes, in order. Every box holds the same type.

beats.say: The square brackets after the type say: this is an array of Strings. The braces list what goes in the boxes, in order. Every box holds the same type.

check.prompt: How many boxes does this array have?
check.why: One box for each value listed in the braces: Ale, Cider and Tea.

steps.say: Each box has a position, called its index — and the first index is 0, not 1.

beats.say: Each box has a position, called its index. And the first index is 0, not 1.

beats.code:
System.out.println(drinks[0]);    // Ale
System.out.println(drinks[1]);    // Cider
System.out.println(drinks[2]);    // Tea

check.why: Counting starts at 0, so index 1 is the SECOND box.

steps.say: drinks.length says how many boxes there are. So the last box is always at length - 1. Ask for a box past the end and the program crashes.

beats.say: drinks.length says how many boxes there are: 3. So the last box is always at index length - 1.
Ask for drinks[3] and the program crashes while it is running: there is no such box.

check.prompt: An array has 10 boxes. What is the index of the last one?
check.why: The indexes run from 0 to 9. That is ten boxes, and the last index is one less than the length.

steps.say: A box can be given a new value, just like any other variable.

beats.say: And a box can be given a new value, just like any other variable.

beats.code:
int[] stock = {50, 25, 30};
stock[0] = stock[0] - 5;      // the first box now holds 45

outro: “Index from 0, last at length - 1. The next monsters will try to make you count from 1.”

question:
int[] a = {5, 8, 15, 16};

Match each expression to its value.
feedback: Indices start at 0, so a[0] is the first element, 5. a.length is the number of elements, 4, which makes a[a.length - 1] the last element, a[3] = 16. a[1] + a[2] adds two elements: 8 + 15 = 23. An index can be any int expression: a[0] - 3 is 2, so a[a[0] - 3] is a[2] = 15.

question: Every box of an array has to hold the same type. Which of these lines compiles?
incorrect: String[] mixed = {"Ale", 25, true};
double[] prices = (3.5, 4.0);
feedback: An array's type is fixed when it is declared, and every value in the braces has to fit it. A String array cannot hold a number or a boolean, and "50" in quotes is text, not an int. The list of values goes in braces, not round brackets.

question: Which of these lines compile and create an array of three ints?
feedback: Braces list the starting values; new int[3] makes three slots that each start at 0; new int[]{...} combines the two. Parentheses and square brackets are not array syntax in Java (square-bracket lists are Python and JavaScript). The size never goes on the left: the type is just int[], and the length belongs to the array object that new or the braces create.

correct: It compiles, then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the second line runs
incorrect: It does not compile: the compiler can see that index 3 is out of range
It compiles and runs: the array grows to make room for a fourth element
It compiles and runs: a write outside the array is silently ignored
feedback: new int[3] makes exactly three slots, numbered 0, 1 and 2, so index 3 does not exist. The compiler does not check index values, even literal ones, so the mistake surfaces only at run time, as an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: "Index 3 out of bounds for length 3". A Java array never grows (that is what ArrayList is for), and Java never quietly ignores a bad index.

question:
Complete the loop header so that it works for an int[] named scores of any size:

for (int i = 0; i < scores.___; i++)
feedback: Every array carries its size in a field called length, written with no parentheses: scores.length. A String, in contrast, has a method, text.length(), with parentheses, and the lists you will meet later use size(). Writing scores.length() or scores.size() for an array does not compile.

question:
int[] nums = new int[{{n}}];

Which index does the expression  nums[nums.length - {{k}}]  refer to? (Give the index, not the value stored there.)
feedback_template: nums.length is {{n}}, so the index is {{n}} - {{k}} = {{expected}}. Since the last valid index is always length - 1, counting back from length is the standard way to reach elements at the end of an array. nums[nums.length] itself is one past the end and throws an exception.

question: One box of the array is given a new value. What does this program print?
feedback: stock[0] is the first box, holding 50. The right-hand side is worked out first — 50 - 5 is 45 — and the result is stored back in the same box. The other two boxes are untouched.

question:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { body }

Put the first five things that happen when this loop runs into order, earliest first.
items: i < 3 is tested while i is 0
The body runs while i is 0
i < 3 is tested while i is 1
feedback: The initialization runs once. After that the loop cycles: test the condition, run the body, run the update, and back to the test. The condition is tested before the very first pass, so a for loop can run zero times, and the update happens after the body, never before it.

question: NPC: Counting the passes of a loop
intro: Nia holds up one hand, fingers folded. “Most loop bugs are the same bug: the loop runs one time too many, or one too few. So we count. On fingers, if we must.”

beats.say: How many times does this bell ring?
Do not guess. List the values i takes while the condition i <= 6 is true: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

check.prompt: How many values are in that list?
check.why: Count them: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 is five values, so the body runs five times.

steps.say: The trap is to subtract: 6 - 2 is 4. But both ends are included, the 2 and the 6. So with <= the number of passes is end - start + 1.

beats.say: The trap is to subtract: 6 - 2 is 4. But both ends are included, the 2 and the 6. So with <= the number of passes is end - start + 1.

steps.say:
Now change <= to < and the last value is lost: i takes 2, 3, 4, 5. With < the number of passes is simply end - start.
Being wrong by exactly one like this has a name: an off-by-one error. The cure is always the same. Write out the first value and the last value that really get used.

beats.say: Now change <= to < and the last value is lost: i takes 2, 3, 4, 5. With < the number of passes is simply end - start.
Being wrong by exactly one like this has a name: an off-by-one error. The cure is always the same. Write out the first value and the last value that really get used.

check.prompt: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)  How many passes?
check.why: i takes 0 through 9. With <, the count is end - start: 10 - 0 = 10.

outro: “A monster ahead will hand you a loop with numbers of its own. First value, last value, then count.”

feedback_template: i takes every value from {{a}} up to and including {{b}}, because the condition is <=. Both ends count, so the number of passes is {{b}} - {{a}} + 1 = {{expected}}. Subtracting without the + 1 is the classic off-by-one error.
i += 2 adds 2 after every pass, so i takes 0, 2, 4 and so on. The condition is i < {{n}}, so the last value printed is {{last}}; {{n}} itself is not. Listing the values gives {{expected}} of them.

question: A for loop visits every box of an array. What does this program print? (Keep the line breaks.)
feedback: d.length is 2, so i takes 0 and then 1. On each pass, i is the index and d[i] is what is in that box. When i reaches 2 the condition 2 < 2 is false, so the loop stops without ever asking for d[2], which does not exist.

question: int[] a holds four values, and each loop below uses a[i] in its body. Which header visits every element exactly once without crashing?
incorrect: for (int i = 0; i <= a.length; i++)
for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++)
for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++)
for (int i = a.length; i > 0; i--)
feedback: Valid indices run from 0 to a.length - 1. Starting at 0 with i < a.length covers exactly those. Using <= reaches a[4], which throws. Starting at 1 misses the first element, and stopping at a.length - 1 with < misses the last. The backwards loop starts at a[4], which throws at once; a correct one runs from a.length - 1 down to i >= 0.

question: Arrange these lines into a program that adds up the array and prints 27.
feedback: The array has to exist before sum can be started from nums[0]; the loop then adds the remaining elements, from index 1 up to the last valid index (i < nums.length); and the total is printed only after the closing brace, once the loop has finished. Printing inside the loop would show a running total three times over.

question: This loop adds up everything in an array. What does the program print?
feedback: total starts at 0 and each pass adds the next box to it: 45, then 53, then 78. The println is after the closing brace, so it runs once, when the loop has finished. Starting the total before the loop is what lets it survive from one pass to the next.

question: A block should repeat while count is less than 10, and the block itself increases count. Which header does that?
incorrect: while (count < 10); {
while (count =< 10) {
while count < 10 {
feedback: The condition goes in parentheses and the block follows directly. The version with a semicolon compiles, which is what makes it dangerous: the ; is an empty statement and becomes the entire loop body, so count never changes and the program hangs forever without reaching the block. =< is not an operator (it is <=, and that would run one extra pass). Leaving out the parentheses is legal in Python and Swift but not in Java.

feedback_template: Trace count: it starts at {{start}} and grows by {{step}} each pass, and the loop goes on while count is still below {{limit}}. The condition is tested before every pass, so the loop ends at the first value that is {{limit}} or more, after {{expected}} passes. count does not have to land exactly on the limit; it only has to stop being less than it.

correct: Prints 0 forever, since count never changes
incorrect: Prints 0 to 4 and then stops as intended
Prints nothing, since the test is false
Prints 0 one time and then stops by itself
feedback: Nothing inside the loop changes count, so 0 < 5 is true on every check and the loop never ends: an infinite loop. A while loop has no built-in counter. Something in its body — here, count++ — has to move it toward the point where the condition becomes false.

question: This while loop keeps going only while both of its conditions hold. What does the program print?
feedback: served goes 1, 2, 3. On the third pass the if sets open to false. The condition is checked again before the next pass: open is false, so open && served < 5 is false and the loop ends — even though served < 5 is still true. && needs both.

question: A while loop with an if-else inside it, and integer division. What single number is printed?
feedback: Even values are halved and odd values become 3n + 1, so n goes 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. That is eight changes, and steps counts one per pass, so 8 is printed. The loop ends when n reaches 1 because 1 > 1 is false. Nobody can tell in advance how many passes this takes, which is why it is a while loop and not a counted for loop.

question: NPC: A method has to answer every time
intro: Nia chalks a method on the wall and then draws a line straight through it. “Now that your code can choose and repeat, Java asks one more thing of a method. Watch what it refuses.”

steps.say: The rounds work as before: I give the first line of a method, you write what goes between the braces, and you return the answer. Run is free; only Submit counts.

beats.say: The rounds work as before. I give you the first line of a method; you write what goes between the braces and return the answer.
Press Run as often as you like: I call your method with each example and show what came back. Only Submit puts you back in the fight.

steps.say: Here is the one Java refuses. If score is 30, the if is skipped — and the method ends with nothing to hand back. Java will not run a method that can end that way.

beats.say: Here is the one Java refuses.
If score is 30, the if is skipped, and the method reaches its closing brace with nothing to hand back. Java checks for this before running anything, and reports a missing return.

check.prompt: What makes Java accept this method?
check.why: Every way through the method has to end at a return. A return placed after the if catches every score the if let through; printing hands nothing back, and another if could be skipped just the same.

steps.say: A return also ends the method on the spot. So once a case has returned, the lines below it only ever see what is left — which often saves you an else.

beats.say: A return also ends the method on the spot. Nothing below it runs.
So once a case has returned, the lines below it only ever see what is left. The same goes for a loop: return in the middle of one and the loop is over.

check.prompt: With that body, what does verdict(75) hand back?
check.why: 75 >= 60 is true, so return "pass" runs — and that ends the method. The last line is never reached, so there is no second answer.

outro: “Ifs, conditions joined with && and ||, loops and arrays, one small method each. Make sure every path through each of them ends at a return.”

question: The ferry charges by age. Return "child" for anyone under 12, "senior" for anyone 65 or over, and "adult" for everyone else.
hint: Return from inside an if for each special case, and let the last line return the ordinary one.
feedback: Deal with the special cases first and let the ordinary one be the return at the end: that last line is also what satisfies Java that every path returns. The boundaries are the cases worth testing — 11 and 12, 64 and 65.

question: The vault opens for anyone of level 10 or higher. It also opens for anyone of level 5 or higher who carries the key. Return true if the vault opens.
signature: public boolean canEnter(int level, boolean hasKey)
hint: There are two ways in. Write each as a test, and join them with ||.
feedback: Two ways in, joined by ||; the second way needs two things at once, joined by &&. && is applied before || anyway, but the parentheses say what you mean. A boolean variable is already true or false: hasKey, not hasKey == true.

question: A health bar shows a number from 0 to 100. Return n unchanged if it is in that range, 0 if it is below it, and 100 if it is above it.
hint: Two ifs that each return at once, then a plain return n for everything in between.
feedback: Each if returns at once, so by the last line n is known to be neither too small nor too large. The same thing can be written as one expression with two ?: operators, but three plain returns are easier to check.

question: A drink costs 6 coins — except during happy hour, when it costs 3. Happy hour runs from hour 17 up to, but not including, hour 19. Return the price at the given hour.
hint: Happy hour is two tests joined with &&. Return 3 inside the if, and 6 after it.
feedback: A range is two comparisons joined by &&, one for each end. The boundaries are what the tests probe: 17 is in, 19 is out. The ordinary price is the plain return at the end, reached whenever the if did not return.

question: Return the sum of the odd numbers from 1 up to and including n: for 6 that is 1 + 3 + 5. If n is less than 1, return 0.
hint: Keep a total that starts at 0 before the loop. A loop can step by 2: i += 2.
feedback: The total is declared before the loop so that it still exists after it. Stepping by 2 from 1 visits only the odd numbers; a loop over every number with an if (i % 2 != 0) inside does the same job. When n is below 1 the loop never runs and 0 is already right.

question: Return how many times n has to be halved, dropping any fraction each time, before it reaches 1. 10 goes 5, 2, 1, which is 3 halvings. n is at least 1.
hint: A while loop that goes on while n is greater than 1, halving n and counting each pass.
feedback: Nobody can say in advance how many passes this takes, so it is a while loop, not a counted for. Integer division does the "dropping any fraction" for you, and the loop must change n on every pass or it never ends.

question: Return the last score in an array. The array will have at least one score in it.
hint: The last index is one less than the number of boxes.
feedback: Indexes start at 0, so the last one is length - 1, never length. For an array, length has no parentheses. Asking for scores[scores.length] would crash: that is one box past the end.

question: Return how many of the scores in an array are greater than the limit. A score equal to the limit does not count.
signature: public int countAbove(int[] scores, int limit)
hint: Start a counter at 0, visit every index from 0 while i < scores.length, and add 1 whenever scores[i] is greater than the limit.
feedback: The counting pattern: start at 0 before the loop, add 1 inside it when the test passes, return after it. The loop runs i from 0 while i < scores.length, so it visits every box and never steps past the last one; for an empty array it never runs at all.
